decision.explanation: Let f(x,y,z)=x^2yz+xy^2z+xyz^2. At (1,-1,1), its partial derivatives are f_x=-2, f_y=0, and f_z=-2. The tangent hyperplane is w+1=-2(x-1)-2(z-1), which simplifies to 2x+2z+w-3=0.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={x}^{2}yz+x{y}^{2}z+xy{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,-1,1,-1).$
after.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}yz+x{y}^{2}z+xy{z}^{2})=2xyz+{y}^{2}z+y{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}yz+x{y}^{2}z+xy{z}^{2})={x}^{2}z+2xyz+x{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}yz+x{y}^{2}z+xy{z}^{2})={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+2xyz\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)(-1)(1)+(-1)^{2}(1)+(-1)(1)^{2}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =(1)^{2}(1)+2(1)(-1)(1)+(1)(1)^{2}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =(1)^{2}(-1)+(1)(-1)^{2}+2(1)(-1)(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-(-1) & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) \\ w+1 & =-2(x-1)+0\cdot (y+1)-2(z-1) \\ w+1 & =-2x-2z+4 \\ 2x+2z+w-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={x}^{2}yz+x{y}^{2}z+xy{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,-1,1,-1).$
content.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}yz+x{y}^{2}z+xy{z}^{2})=2xyz+{y}^{2}z+y{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}yz+x{y}^{2}z+xy{z}^{2})={x}^{2}z+2xyz+x{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}yz+x{y}^{2}z+xy{z}^{2})={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+2xyz\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)(-1)(1)+(-1)^{2}(1)+(-1)(1)^{2}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =(1)^{2}(1)+2(1)(-1)(1)+(1)(1)^{2}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =(1)^{2}(-1)+(1)(-1)^{2}+2(1)(-1)(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-(-1) & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) \\ w+1 & =-2(x-1)+0\cdot (y+1)-2(z-1) \\ w+1 & =-2x-2z+4 \\ 2x+2z+w-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{xyz}$ at the point $(2,2,4,4).$
content.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xyz})=\frac{\sqrt{yz}}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xyz})=\frac{\sqrt{xz}}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xyz})=\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,2,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,4) & =\frac{\sqrt{2\cdot 4}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,4) & =\frac{\sqrt{2\cdot 4}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,4) & =\frac{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}}{2\sqrt{4}}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-4 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,4)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,4)+(z-4)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,4) \\ w-4 & =(x-2)+(y-2)+\frac{1}{2}(z-4) \\ w-4 & =x+y+\frac{z}{2}-6 \\ -x-y-\frac{z}{2}+w+2 & =0 \\ 2x+2y+z-2w-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: A normal to the tangent plane is (ln(y), x/y+2y, -1). For it to be parallel to (0,2,-2), its third component fixes the proportionality factor at 1/2. Thus ln(y)=0 and x/y+2y=1. These give y=1, x=-1, and z=1. Hence the unique point is (-1,1,1).

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: At which points on the surface $z=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨0,2,-2⟩?$
after.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{x}{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨0,2,-2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨0,2,-2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}c\operatorname{ln}⁡y=0 \\ \frac{cx}{y}+2cy=2 \\ -c=-2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2\operatorname{ln}⁡y=0\,⟹\,y=1.
$$

And substituting $c=2$ and $y=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
\frac{2x}{1}+2(2)(1)=2\,⟹\,x=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-1$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =(-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{1}^{2} \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-1,1,1).$

after.problem: At which point on the surface $z=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v=⟨4,-2,-1⟩?$
after.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=6x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨4,-2,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩=⟨4,-2,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}6cx=4 \\ 2cy=-2 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
6(1)x=4\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
2(1)y=-2\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\frac{2}{3}$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+(-1)^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+1 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3}).$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is ⟨6x,2y,−1⟩.

From the third equation, we get c=1. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 6(1)x=4⟹x=23.

Finally, substituting x=23 and y=−1 into our function, we get z=3(23)2+(−1)2=43+1=73.

content.problem: At which point on the surface $z=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v=⟨4,-2,-1⟩?$
content.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=6x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨4,-2,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩=⟨4,-2,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}6cx=4 \\ 2cy=-2 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
6(1)x=4\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
2(1)y=-2\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\frac{2}{3}$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+(-1)^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+1 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3}).$
